title: Schedule the application of water to plants and landscapes

lessons.title: How much water plants need and when
lessons.html:
How much water plants need

A watering schedule says when to water, how long and which area. A good schedule gives plants enough water to grow well, without wasting water. Too little water makes plants wilt and die. Too much water drowns roots, washes away fertiliser, causes root rot and fungus, and wastes money.

Things that change how much water is needed

  • Weather: hot, sunny, windy days dry plants and soil quickly. Cool, cloudy days need less water. After good rain, you may not need to water at all.
  • Season: plants need more water in summer and less in winter. In winter-rainfall areas like the Western Cape the pattern is different from summer-rainfall areas like Gauteng.
  • Soil type: sandy soil drains fast and needs water more often but in smaller amounts. Clay soil holds water longer but takes water in slowly, so water it more slowly and less often.
  • Plant type: lawns, vegetables, seedlings and new plants need more frequent water. Established trees, succulents and many indigenous plants need less.
  • Shade and sun: plants in full sun dry faster than plants in shade.
  • Mulch: mulched beds stay moist longer.

Deep and less often

For most established plants and lawns, it is better to water deeply and less often than a little every day. Deep watering makes roots grow down, so plants survive dry periods better. Shallow daily watering keeps roots near the surface.

When to water

  • Early morning is best: cool, little wind, and leaves dry quickly in the day, which reduces fungus.
  • Late afternoon is second best.
  • Avoid midday: much of the water evaporates.
  • Avoid windy times with sprinklers.

Checking the soil

Push a finger, a trowel or a soil probe into the soil. If the soil is dry a few centimetres down, it is time to water. If it is still moist, wait.

lessons.title: Making and following a watering schedule
lessons.html:
Making a watering schedule

Steps

  1. Divide the site into zones with similar needs: lawns, sunny beds, shady beds, new plantings, pots, indigenous areas. Each irrigation valve or station usually waters one zone.
  2. Decide how often each zone needs water, based on plant type, soil, sun and season.
  3. Decide how long to water each time, so water reaches the roots without running off. Check with a trowel how deep the water went after a run.
  4. Choose the time of day: early morning, one zone after another so the water pressure stays good.
  5. Follow water restrictions. Municipalities often limit watering days and times. These rules must be followed.
  6. Write it down in a table or set it on the irrigation controller.

Example schedule (summer, sandy soil)

ZoneDaysTime
1 Front lawnMon, Wed, Fri05:00
2 Sunny bedsMon, Thu05:30
3 Shady bedsTue06:00
4 New plantingsDaily for the first weeks06:15

Run times depend on the sprinkler type and water pressure on your site; your supervisor will set them.

Adjusting the schedule

  • Switch off or skip a cycle after rain. Rain sensors can do this automatically.
  • Increase water during heat waves; reduce it in winter.
  • Watch the plants: wilting, yellowing or puddles tell you something is wrong.
  • Check that sprinklers and drippers work, are not blocked, and do not spray onto paving or walls.

Recording

Keep a simple record of watering, rain and any problems. This helps plan, saves water, and shows the client the site is managed well.

Key points

  • Weather, season, soil, plant type and sun all affect water needs.
  • Water deeply and less often for established plants.
  • Water early in the morning and check the soil before watering.
  • Divide the site into zones and set days, times and run times for each.
  • Follow water restrictions and adjust the schedule for rain and season.
